name: journal-did-paul-call-jesus-god.json
content:
Did Paul call ʿĪsā ibn Maryam (ʿalayhi al-salām, peace be upon him) God? Where he names God and the Christ in the same sentence, I find that he keeps them apart. Three passages show it most plainly, two in 1 Timothy and one in 1 Corinthians.

In the first, Paul charges Timothy "in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus and of the elect angels".1 Three parties are named in a row, and the word "God" falls on the first of them alone. A reader who took Christ Jesus to be God would have no reason to set the two names side by side as if they were two.

The second is longer. "I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus ... until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he will display at the proper time."2 Again God is the one who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus is named after him. The appearing of ʿĪsā is an event that God will display, in the time God chooses.

A caution belongs here. Both passages come from 1 Timothy, one of the three Pastoral letters, and many scholars doubt that Paul wrote them.3 For a reader who holds the letter to be Paul's, the words are his. For one who does not, they come from a later writer who used his name. Either way the church has read them as Paul's, and they are the church's own text.

The third passage comes from a letter nobody disputes. In 1 Corinthians 15 Paul describes the end: "When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all."4 The Son is subjected, and the one he is subjected to is God. Paul closes the sentence on God, with no remainder.

Earlier in the same letter he divides the two titles outright: "for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist."5 The title God goes to the Father, and the title Lord to Jesus Christ.

Does "Lord" settle the matter the other way? By itself it does not. The Greek word kyrios serves for a master, for a man addressed with respect, and for the divine name in the Greek scriptures.6 What decides its sense in Paul is the company it keeps. At the end of the great hymn in Philippians every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord, and the hymn ends "to the glory of God the Father".7

The verdict

On the evidence of these passages, Paul uses the name God for the Father and sets Christ Jesus beside him, below him and subject to him. He never writes in the seven letters accepted as his that ʿĪsā is God, with one disputed exception that I take up below.

A Christian reader will answer with other verses, and the answers deserve a hearing. They are met in the questions that follow. Where the texts divide, I say so, and I leave the reader to weigh them.

Did Paul call ʿĪsā God?: questions readers ask

Does Paul ever call Jesus God?

The two verses most often given are Romans 9:5 and Titus 2:13. In Romans the Greek can be read two ways, and translators divide.8 Titus is a Pastoral letter, and its phrase "our great God and Savior Jesus Christ" can also be read as two persons, "our great God" and "Savior Jesus Christ".9

What about Philippians 2:6, "in the form of God"?

Christians read it as a claim to deity. The passage goes on to say that God highly exalted him and gave him the name above every name, and it ends with the glory of God the Father. A being who is exalted by another and glorifies another stands below him in the very verses that are quoted for his equality.

Does "Lord" mean God?

Not by itself. The same word is used of Abraham by Sarah, and in 1 Corinthians 8:5 Paul himself writes of "many 'lords'".11 Where he wants to speak of the one God he says "the Father".

Did Paul write Hebrews, where Jesus prays?

Hebrews does not say who wrote it, and the early church doubted that it was Paul. It tells of ʿĪsā that in the days of his flesh he "offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death".10 The verse is worth reading, but it is not Paul's voice and I do not cite it as his.

Why does this matter?

Because the doctrine of the Trinity is said to rest on the apostles. If the apostle who wrote most of the New Testament keeps God and Christ apart in the very sentences where he names them, the reader is entitled to ask where the doctrine came from. The Qurʾān says that ʿĪsā was a messenger of God (al-Nisāʾ 4:171).

  1. 1 Timothy 5:21 (ESV). ↩
  2. 1 Timothy 6:13–15 (ESV). The verses continue, "the blessed and only Sovereign, the King of kings and Lord of lords, who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see" (6:15–16). Most commentators take this to be God the Father, since many people saw ʿĪsā. ↩
  3. On the Pastoral letters and the question of their author, see [paulus_link slug="thirteen-letters-or-fourteen" /]. ↩
  4. 1 Corinthians 15:28 (ESV). ↩
  5. 1 Corinthians 8:5–6 (ESV). ↩
  6. Peter writes that Sarah "obeyed Abraham, calling him lord" (1 Peter 3:6, ESV). The Greek word is the same kyrios. ↩
  7. Philippians 2:9–11 (ESV). ↩
  8. Romans 9:5. The Greek has no punctuation. One reading ends the sentence at "the Christ" and gives the rest to God as a blessing ("God who is over all be blessed forever"); the other reads "the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever". Translators and commentators divide. ↩
  9. Titus 2:13. Titus is one of the Pastoral letters. ↩
  10. Hebrews 5:7 (ESV). The letter names no author, and the early church doubted that Paul wrote it. ↩
  11. Compare note 6, and 1 Corinthians 8:5 above. ↩
